newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: WA premier signals push for fundamental tax reform.
newsitem.headline: WA premier signals push for fundamental tax reform.

text.p: Western Australia's premier, Richard Court, on Tuesday raised the prospect of a new push by the states for fundamental tax reform following last week's Premier's Conference.
Court told reporters he supported the view that all tax reform options, including a state-based sales tax, should be considered.
"I've said on many many occasions it would be irresponsible not to address tax reform by putting all options on the table," he said.

"Currently the states are preparing some tax options and we are going to present those publicly when they are completed and I am sure they are going to look at all the different arrangements including (state-based sales tax).
"It is ludicrous that the states do not have responsibility for raising the revenue they are spending.
"So we want to look at all of those options and hopefully by the end of the year we will have that options paper completed."

At last week's Premiers' Conference Prime Minister John Howard announced further cuts in tied grants to the states as well as reduced general assistance. Western Australia will get a total of A$3.41 billion next fiscal year, down A$56.9 million.
Court's tax reform comments were prompted by a question about whether Western Australia would consider levying a state-based sales tax if the opportunity to do so arose.

The High Court is currently considering an attempt by the states to overturn the prevailing interpretation of Section 90 of the Australian Constitution which gives the Commonwealth exclusive power to "impose duties of customs and ... excise".
According to that interpretation, which is based on a 1949 High Court decision known as Parton's case, the Commonwealth's power is so broad it precludes the states from levying sales taxes.

In the latest High Court case, a New South Wales tobacco wholesaler and two duty-free store operators claim NSW licence fees are actually excises and, by virtue of Parton's case, are beyond NSW's power to levy.
In response, Queensland, Tasmania, South Australia, the Northern Territory, Western Australia and the ACT have joined NSW in challenging Parton's case.
The states raise some A$5 billion a year from licence fees but NSW argued in its oral submission to the High Court that this form of taxation was "becoming increasingly uncollectable".
"That particular case is obviously of concern to us," Court said today.
"(However) we have received a commitment from the Prime Minister that regardless of what way that case come down they will protect the state's revenue base from those sources."
"So we have that commitment from the Prime Minister and I think that's important."
